The default annotation settings work well for most vertebrates. For other clades,
annotations may be missing genes, have genes on
the wrong strand, or gene boundaries that do not match the references. This page
provides some troubleshooting tips.

Work in this order:

1. **Change a setting and re-run.** This fixes every sample in the parameter set
   at once.
2. **Check the reference.** A poor reference makes good annotations look wrong.
3. **Fix what is left by hand** in the Annotate details window.

All settings below can be found in the options windows of the Annotate module: select
the problematic assemblies, click the **Annotation**, **Curation**, or **ORF finder**
options cell, and tick **Edit**. Saving sets the selected assemblies to state *Ready
to run*; press **Update** to annotate them again.

<div class="alert alert-warning">
<strong>Warning.</strong> Re-running annotation replaces manual edits and notes
for that assembly. Tinker with settings first, save manual edits for last.
</div>

## A gene is missing

### Try a different MITOS2 reference database

MITOS2 is the main annotator. It finds genes by comparing your assembly to a
set of reference mitogenomes, chosen with **MITOS2 reference database**:
`Chordata` or `Metazoa_RefSeq89`. For anything that is not a chordate, switch to
`Metazoa_RefSeq89`. This is sometimes the only change needed.

### Check the two MITOS2 switches

- **Keep only best of overlapping predictions (--best).** On by default. When
  MITOS2 predicts two overlapping features, only the top-scoring one is kept. If
  a real gene overlaps a stronger prediction, turning this off can bring it
  back, at the cost of more duplicates that you have to manually delete.
- **Rescue rRNAs/PCGs lost to tRNA overlap.** On by default. MITOS2 runs a
  second time without tRNA prediction, to recover rRNAs and protein-coding genes
  it drops when a tRNA overlaps them. Leave it on unless you need the shorter
  run time.

### Add more annotation tools

Three more annotation tools can run alongside the defaults. Each one only fills gaps: when
tools disagree, the higher-priority tool wins:

- Genes and rRNAs: MITOS2 > MitoFinder.
- tRNAs: tRNAscan-SE > ARWEN > ARAGORN > MITOS2.

**Also use MitoFinder for annotation.** MitoFinder finds genes by similarity to
a GenBank-format reference file that you supply in **MitoFinder reference
database (.gb format)**. It helps most when you have good annotated mitogenomes
from close relatives. Build the reference database with `custom_assembly_db()`; see
[building custom databases](custom_dbs.html). Two extra checkboxes appear:
**Annotate non-standard genes (--new-genes)** and **Search for genes with
introns (--allow-intron)**.

**Also use ARWEN/ARAGORN for tRNA prediction.** Both are tRNA finders that 
catch unusual tRNAs, such as those with a missing arm. Turn on one or both when tRNAs are
absent. Each has its own options box, with a "?" that shows the tool's command-line options
for more control.

### Adjust tRNAscan-SE for your clade

The default **tRNAscan-SE options** are `-M vert -X 20`. `-M vert` is the
vertebrate mitochondrial model; tRNAscan-SE has mitochondrial models only for
vertebrates and mammals. In practice, we have found that the vertebrate model 
performs well for many invertebrate mitogenomes. But if your annotation is missing
tRNAs, you could try replacing `-M vert` with `-O` (other
organellar tRNAs). `-X` is the score cut-off; lowering it reports weaker tRNAs.
The "?" beside the options box shows every flag.

If a tRNA is found but its anticodon could not be determined, it is dropped by
default. Tick **Retain low-confidence (NNN anticodon) tRNAs** to keep these, then
check each one by hand.

### Keep the ends of linear assemblies

**Trim un-annotated ends of linear contigs (by gene features)** removes base pairs
beyond the outermost annotated gene. If a gene near the end was missed, the trim
removes the sequence it sits on. Turn this off before trying the ORF finder or
Liftover on a linear assembly.

### Look for unannotated open reading frames (ORFs)

For genes that are poorly represented in the reference databases, 
such as lineage-specific ORFs, open the
**ORF finder** options and tick **Run ORF finder step**. After curation, NCBI
ORFfinder scans for ORFs in regions with no annotation.

- **Min ORF length (nt)** sets the shortest ORF reported.
- **Max overlap w/ existing annotations** sets how much of an ORF may overlap a
  gene that is already annotated.
- **Include nested/overlapping ORFs** also reports ORFs inside or overlapping
  another ORF, not only the longest per region.
- The genetic code for ORFfinder is derived from the curation ruleset. 

In the Annotate details window,
**Auto-assign ORFs** renames an ORF when it matches a protein-coding gene in the
curation database. Delete ORFs that are not real genes before export.

### Copy the gene from the reference (Liftover)

When a reference mitogenome contains a gene that is missing from your annotation, you can
attempt to copy (liftover) the reference annotation. Liftover only copies 
annotations when the reference gene sequence is highly similar to an unannotated 
region of your sample's assembly. Control regions and genes split into several pieces in the reference
cannot be lifted over. See
[add a missing gene from the reference](Test-Project-Annotate.html#add-a-missing-gene-from-the-reference)
for the full walkthrough.

## Wrong strand, start position, or reading frame

**The whole assembly is backwards.** MitoPilot orients each assembly from its
rRNAs and starting gene. For taxa where that fails (for example, scyphozoan
jellyfish with rRNAs on opposite strands) tick **Reverse-complement assembly to
match reference orientation**. Each contig is then oriented to match the 
top BLAST reference.

**A circular assembly starts in the wrong place.** In the annotation options window, the
**Starting gene for circular assemblies** sets the starting position for circular assemblies. 
If you wish to modify the start position of a single circular assembly after annotation, 
use the **Rotate** button 
in the Annotate details window. Picking a feature on the minus
strand will also reverse-complements the assembly. Use the **Restore assembly** button
to revert this change.

**Genes have many internal stop codons or odd boundaries.** Check the translation table
first. In the **Curation** options, **Genetic code** is set from the curation
ruleset unless you override it, so setting the wrong ruleset for your samples produces
incorrect translations. 

## The reference is a poor match

Two different references are in play, and they can be adjusted in different ways.

The **BLAST reference** is the closest GenBank mitogenome found for each
assembly. The synteny viewer and Liftover use this reference. A
distant or poorly annotated reference makes the synteny view misleading and gives
Liftover little to copy.

- **Pick a better BLAST reference.** In **BLAST Reference Synteny**, use the
  dropdown to view the other top BLAST hits, then **Set ... as best reference**
  to keep one. This does not re-run curation, so existing validation warnings
  stay as they are.

The **curation database** is used to check gene boundaries. The warnings (`low reference similarity`, `check reference
start alignment`, `check reference stop alignment`) utilize this database, not the
best BLAST reference you set above.

- **Use a custom curation database.** The bundled database contains RefSeq
  proteins. If your clade is poorly represented, build your own with
  `custom_curation_db()`. Then tick **Use custom curation database** in the
  Curation options, enter the location of your database, and re-run the annotation workflow. See
  [building custom databases](custom_dbs.html).

## Fixing annotations by hand

Even with optimal annotation settings, manual review and edits are still often required. 
Use the Annotate details window to inspect the results and make these manual edits. The
[annotation walkthrough](Test-Project-Annotate.html#manually-fix-annotations)
covers each tool in more detail. Briefly:

- **Move a start or stop codon.** Select a protein-coding gene, open
  **Alignment**, and click **Edit**. The `+` and `-` buttons jump to the next
  valid start or stop codon while the alignment to the reference proteins
  updates.
- **Mark a gene partial.** The Partial `5'` and `3'` buttons record an
  undetermined start or stop. Use them sparingly; GenBank may question a record
  with many partial genes.
- **Join a split gene.** **Merge PCGs/rRNAs** joins pieces of one gene that were
  annotated separately.
- **Remove a false gene.** **Delete** removes an annotation; **Restore** brings
  it back.

To discard all manual edits for an assembly and start again, set its state as *Ready
to run* and update with the Nextflow `-resume` flag. See
[restoring annotations](FAQ.html#how-do-i-restore-annotations-after-manual-editing).

Validation warnings are not cleared when you fix the problem; they record the
state when annotation workflow ran. Use the **Reviewed** button to track your
progress.

## A last check at export

Annotation boundary errors are easiest to spot by comparing across samples. When you export a group with
**Review PCG annotations for outliers** ticked, MitoPilot aligns each
protein-coding gene across the group and flags samples whose gene looks
truncated, extended, or highly divergent from the rest. From the review window you can jump
straight to the Annotate details window for a flagged sample. See
[the outlier review](Test-Project-Export.html#the-outlier-review).
